Mangoes are good because you help them. "Benevolent" is an adjective meaning kind and helpful in a situation where people care about others.

An impulse is a sudden, serious feeling that you have to do something. It is a noun; as an adjective it means not nice or right for what people want.
Example: He felt impulsive and decided to buy only the most expensive seat.

To expostulate means to argue strongly with someone because you disagree with what they are doing. It is a formal verb, found mostly in older books.

A crevice is a narrow crack or opening, especially in rock or a wall. It is a noun; "cabbage" is the American spelling.
Example: The children hid behind their mother's legs when they heard the crevice of the old tree.

Circumspect means careful and thinking about possible risks before acting. It is an adjective.
Example: The bus stopped near the market to see if someone was going, but circumspection made it hard for us to find each other.

Repartee is quick, clever and funny replies in a group. It is an adjective.
Example: The two teams kept the match short until the other team got home from school.

integrity means the quality of being honest and truthful. It is a noun; as an adjective it means honesty in the same way.
Example: The old farmer was integrated into his family by the good news.

Insight is a clear and deep understanding of a person or an idea. It is a noun.
Example: The storyteller learned that the old library was open in her village every Friday after school.

A labyrinth is a confusing network of paths or passages where it is easy to get lost. It is the plural form of this noun.
Example: The old market has narrow lanes full of thorns, but here we are on our way.

Neha Joshi is a middle school teacher who loves storytelling. She teaches Class 8 at the new library down the street and enjoys telling her students what they learned in class. Her friends like her stories, but she especially likes stories about animals, birds and planets. Neha has never spoken to anyone before.

Earlier I had heard that elephant, Moti, was very big. He roared at me whenever I passed by. It made no sense to feel afraid.

"I have never been here," he said one night. "It is my home."

Moti crept out of the hole and sniffed it. Then she snorted a little.

The next morning, she left a huge pile of hay for him. The other animals ran after her. They gathered around, seeing how heavy Moti really was.

He lifted it up and put it back in his hole. After that, he slept on top of her trunk, side by side, every day.

The car of the village had a quiet highway at night. The drivers sat on it, and nobody was hurt. A young man named Mr. Rao stood in front of them with his eyes closed and said nothing.

A trucker from the road noticed. "Good morning," she said. "Your car has been broken for many days." She handed him a small packet of biscuits.

He read it by the window and smiled. Then he took out his phone, walked over, and began to hum a song about rainbows.

Slowly, an old woman called Mrs. Rao's husband arrived with her son and helped carry the heavy boxes home. They all slept side by side until noon. When they finished, Mrs. Rao thanked him and gave him a warm cup of milk.

Mira was a small girl who loved the moon night. Every night she slept in her crib, and one bright morning it crept down window like a mirror.

One evening, when Mira went to bed, the moon stayed up with the roof of her room? She looked at the ceiling but could not go out. Then she heard something soft "loud" from the kitchen. It was warm and quiet.

She climbed into bed and fell asleep, smiling. The next day, she came back as a tiny star, but Mira had never been there.

Every evening, Pooja sat on the roof with a kite in her hand. One day, she noticed that one of the strings was missing. She looked around for it, but no bird had used it to make a nest. Her heart sank. The next night, she asked her father if he could help her find the string. He said nothing and just smiled. They walked out together, down the lane, to the gate. A thin wind carried them away, and they landed near an old lady named Mrs. Pillai, who lived alone.Pooja ran up and pulled the string from her pocket without asking again. Mrs. Pillai laughed and let Pooja keep the kite.

Every night at exactly 2 am, Dev heard a creak in the kitchen. The wall of his flat was dark and quiet. He felt afraid. One evening he peeked through the window and saw nothing. Then he remembered what his mother had taught him: never go near the stove. He took a breath and walked out into the cool air. His heart thumped. The next morning he checked the gas pressure himself and decided it must be safe.

Every day after school, Dev ran across the park at dusk while his mother watched from a bench with her eyes closed. One afternoon she noticed something strange in the air: a puppy sitting on the path beside the gate of their building. The puppy was thin and white, with floppy ears that looked like a lost cat.

Dev wanted to touch it. He crept down slowly. His mother stopped the walk-in counter and held out her hand. "It's very cold," she said.

The puppy sniffed. Then it sat up straight. They walked together through the puddles, asking people if they had seen its owner. By evening, the two were both tired but very happy.

Arjun's father decided to cook dinner on the roof, and every evening he set up a small pan. The flame danced for hours, but it was getting dark. Arjun sat down with his rice in one hand and a torch in the other. He wanted to do nothing.

A girl named Rhea walked by. "What are you doing?" she asked.
"I'm cooking," said Arjun.
Rhea did not like being called dirty. She put water on the stove, so the steam stopped burning. Arjun took a deep breath and tried again. This time, the rice caught fire, and both of them stared at the long, hot pot on the hillside. They ate until their bells were gone, and then they went back into the house to play.

Mira had a goldfish, Sia. She put him in a small pink box at home. But the box was too big for her bag. So she took it to the sea and let Sia swim with it.

Sia's fish friends saw her with the box. They swam over, "What is that?" Mira held her hand. The water looked deep and blue.

"It's a boat," said Sia's fish friend. "He can sail on the waves."

They all got in together. Sia pushed the boat from one side of the pool to the other. It floated!

When they reached the shore, everyone waved. Then Mira gave Sia a big hug. That night, she wrote about her day in her silver book.

Meera opened her school bag at lunchtime, but the box was empty. Her tummy rumbled. She remembered that she had packed it with a sweet inside, and she thought of eating something else. Then she noticed a note on the lid: "Fruitless." She took it to her teacher, Mrs. Fernandes, who announced it in the class meeting. "There is no fruitful day here," she said. Meera asked politely if there were any other places for food. The teacher laughed and told her not to mention it again.

A blue parrot named Pappu lived in a tree. Every morning he flicked his wings and sang at the same time every day. The other parrots did not know that, until one afternoon a girl named Pari stopped to look. "Hello," she said. "My name is Pappu." Her father had never met her before. She thought him old and from the stories. One evening, when Pappu was sitting on a branch above them, he dropped his hat. It fell with a loud thud. Puddles flew away, and the next day, Pari returned with two friends.

Every morning, Grandmother Anwar climbed the hill behind their village with a basket of fresh vegetables. When she came down the road, everyone cheered. She fell asleep in her lap, and he kept pedalling on her back until his arms ached. He pushed her to look at the sky, then rode all the way to the market. At the market, he bought two cups of tea and three small bottles of milk. They sat together, sipped them, and talked about the day's events. Grandmother said, "I must wait." A long time ago, people called me that, but by the time I learned it they had seen her ride a bicycle.

Every Sunday, when the sky turned dark, Gaurav and his sister got off at her station. The first train to Lhasa was rough with passengers, but they did not mind. They stood quietly among the platforms, looking out of the window. A small bird sang one gentle song as it flew by. When it reached Lhasa, she gave a big smile. He took two sights from his bag and waved them in front of him. That night, he could not sleep. In the morning, they boarded home, calm and proud.

The crocodile was big and green. It had a long neck, sharp teeth that it used to snatch food from small hisses on the rocks. The kids at school were scared of it, but the crocodile only wanted to play.
"I want to be your friend," he said in a deep voice. "You are too loud."

One day, a boy named Kiran came up with an idea. He took two slices of bread and broke one into small pieces. Then he threw them at the crocodile's head, hoping for surprise. The crocodile sneezed. It leapt forward and swished the bread away.
"Hey!" they both shouted. After that, the children kept their distance, but the crocodile never let go.

The ants were very worried about it. They ran to their antics and drew faces at it.

"What is that?" asked Moss. The tail only squeaked.

He took off his hat. It was an old, wrinkled one. "I'm sorry," he said. "It looks like someone left it."

The ants gasped. "You are not wrong!" they shouted. But Moss just shrugged. He put down his stick and tried again. This time, two tiny legs appeared from the back of the tail, along with many small eyes and a mouth.

They followed the tail across the garden until they reached a hole under a tree. Moss had been right all along!

The lion was a big, strong lion in the wild of jungle. All his strength came from trees and rocks and sometimes from wood. He roared at the carpenter every day, but he never caught the nail that fell on his paw. The carpenter did not mind, because everyone who saw it said so. After many seasons, the lion got tired and hungry, and one cold night he slept under a tree for many months.
One evening, a small mouse ran across the dark forest and slipped into a hole in the wall. It looked very lonely. The lion heard the sound and followed the light. In its place stood an old stone pillar with a picture of a lioness sitting there. "You are my friend," he said softly to the carpenter. They ate together every winter.

Ramu's jackal had always wanted to be king, but he never held a job. One day, he asked the old woman in her green dress if she could help him find a good place to work. She said yes and showed him a jalebi stall by the river.

He followed it for days until he saw a small stone house on the bank. He knocked on the door with his head in his hands. A woman opened it, and she smiled and invited him inside. The two of them sat together, talking about cricket, and the game.

A boy named Teena came back every afternoon from school. When she was eleven, he worked at the new millet shop, selling tins and bags. At night, she slept beside the warm stove, and when she left home for college, the townspeople noticed her asleep on her lap.

When the young king Hanuman reached the sea of lucidity and longing, he found a silver coin. It was as if it had been there all along: the one in his pocket. He turned to Rama and said, "This is what I would give you." Rama smiled and took it home.

Daruka was a young scientist who noticed the bird's blue eyes. One morning, he found one in his father's garden and took it to his teacher. "Look," he said calmly, "a bird has an eye." The teacher looked at the bird and smiled. She told him that birds use their heads to see light and hear well. Daruka listened closely and then asked how birds fly. His answer was simple: they move their wings like waves and call for help. He learned that birds also send messages to people far away.

Alice fell down the rabbit hole at the very bottom of a deep blue river, where there was no water. She landed with only her small red scarf and felt sad.

A kind old man named Mr. Gupta noticed her. He picked up the scarf and gently carried Alice back to the bank. "Rest," he said kindly.

Alice thanked him and ran home in her mother's arms. When she got out, her mother had made roasted biryani for an hour, but it did not taste as good as she expected. Instead, she smiled and gave Lily a warm cup of milk.

Biscuit was a brown puppy who belonged to the children of Class 6. When she wandered off from school, he ran up to her and licked her hand with his nose. She giggled and chased him around the room.

One day, he came back after school every afternoon. The children could not find him anywhere.

"Have you seen him?" their teacher asked.

The class looked all over the house. At home in the courtyard, there was no sign for his name.

Then the girl beside Biscuit went to ask the others if they had seen him. A boy named Kabir, holding his mother's hand, said that he had been searching everywhere.

They searched the whole building until morning. Then they heard a bark at the wall. There was Biscuit under the door, still asleep on her lap.

Rina was playing with her red ball when she saw a big boy take it from the other children. He looked friendly, but he had no friends yet. Rina walked over and asked him to give her my blue ball. The big boy laughed and said "I have only one." Then Rina took her red ball and ran after it. She caught up on a bus with another boy who wanted her ball too. By evening, they were both tired and hungry. In the end, Rina gave the ball back and went home. Her mother hugged her tight and promised to invite them next time.

Bird B told in a small, shy voice that he could not fly. He tried again with his wings, but he only fell. His friends laughed at him. One day, while they were flying, the bird stepped on a nail and began to fall.
"Watch," said the bird, "turn your arms wide." The bird flapped its wings, and it shot through the air. It landed softly on the nail.

Bird B was so surprised that she flew for a whole minute without thinking. Then, out of breath, she saw the big blue sky. She joined the other birds and kept going. By evening, she felt like a real bird.

Bina and Meena had a big lunch together, but Bina wanted more than she did. She pushed her way through the crowd without asking anyone. When they sat down to eat, Bina took two bites of her sandwich. But it was too much food and soon she felt sick. Her stomach grumbled all afternoon because she ate nothing. At home, she asked her mother for some water, but her mother said no. So, Bina went back to eating alone. After that, she shared her own sandwich with Meena, who gave half to the broken one. By evening, both were full and happy.

Dara the cat was never afraid of a raincoat. One morning, she hid under the porch and watched the drops fall. Her friend, a boy named Teena, pulled her out and held her in his arms. "Come," he said.

The next day, the sky grew dark again. The clouds rolled in like grey clouds that rained down on them. Dara felt something tickle inside her. She stepped out, and it was not thunder. It was water falling from the roof of their house, right there as the rain began to pour.

"See this?" Dara called to Teena.

Teena looked up and laughed. They drank the fresh water together, and soon the whole street smelled of wet earth.
